344.title: The prayer at the foundations
344.hook: Ibrahim and Isma'il pray for a messenger from among the people (2:127–129)
344.carry: pray for the ones not born
344.tomorrow: What will you worship after me
344.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ibrahim and Isma'il's words, Rabbana taqabbal minna, our Lord, accept from us, after completing a good deed, and pray for their children and for generations to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim tested, and your line, tested, then trusted. Did you finish the hard duty, or take its last step? Today, Ibrahim again, with stones in his hands. Day three hundred forty-four.

Old buildings sometimes have a time capsule sealed into a cornerstone: a newspaper, a few coins, a letter addressed to whoever opens it in a hundred years. The builders will never meet that reader. They write anyway. In al-Baqarah, a father and son are raising the foundations of a house in a dry valley in Arabia. As they lift the stones, they speak, and much of what they say is for people who don't exist yet. Today: the prayer at the foundations.
screen: `A LETTER IN THE CORNERSTONE.` → `A FATHER AND SON, LIFTING STONES.` → `WORDS FOR PEOPLE NOT YET BORN.`

segments.voice: Last year you watched Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the Kaaba. This year, listen to what they were saying while they did it. Verse one hundred twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.” They're building God's house, and their first words ask that it be accepted, as if it might not be. Then the prayer grows. Make us both submissive to You, they ask, and from our descendants a nation submissive to You. Show us our rites, and turn to us. And then, in verse one hundred twenty-nine, the furthest request: Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves, who will recite Your verses to them, teach them the book and wisdom, and purify them. Think about the distance in that prayer. Muslims hold that it was answered thousands of years later, in the same valley, in Mecca, with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has him say: I am the answer to the prayer of my father Ibrahim, and the good news of Isa. The scholars notice the order inside the prayer, too. Accept what we did. Make us good. Make our children good. Send them a teacher. It moves outward, from the two of them to people they'd never see. The stones they lifted are long hidden under later rebuildings. The prayer is still being read, in this surah, every day. Pray for the ones not born.
screen: `OUR LORD! ACCEPT FROM US` · `FROM US, TO OUR DESCENDANTS` · `A MESSENGER FROM AMONG THEM` · `I AM THE ANSWER TO IBRAHIM'S PRAYER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those who come after you. Think of people you'll never meet, or barely will: grandchildren, your students' students, whoever lives in your home after you, a child born this year somewhere far away. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can use the builders' own first words, Our Lord, accept from us, and then ask good for them in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
The prayer at the foundations. Ibrahim and Isma'il, raising the House, asking for acceptance, for good descendants, and for a messenger to come. Today's word.
screen: `THE PRAYER AT THE FOUNDATIONS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pray for the ones not born. Today, do one thing whose good you won't see: plant something, save something, teach something. Day three hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 344 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WILL YOU WORSHIP AFTER ME.`

fork.reveal: accept from us: they ask for acceptance, as if the work might not be enough, then pray outward to their descendants.

what it means: a prayer said while building, reaching out to people thousands of years away.
what a scholar hears: the prayer of 2:129, a messenger who recites, teaches the book and wisdom, and purifies, which Muslims hold was answered in Muhammad, as the hadith in Ahmad says.

345.title: What will you worship after me
345.word: What will you worship after me
345.hook: the dying Ya'qub asks his sons, and they answer, your God and the God of your fathers (2:133)
345.carry: what will you keep after me
345.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to prepare a wasiyyah, a will, and many add words of counsel for their families about faith and conduct, following the example of Ibrahim and Ya'qub in al-Baqarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer at the foundations, and your line: pray for the ones not born. Ibrahim prayed for his descendants. Today, two generations on, one of them is dying. Day three hundred forty-five.

People who've sat with someone near the end often say the same thing: the last conversations are short, and they're about what matters. Nobody asks about the mortgage. They ask: are you going to be all right? Will you look after your sister? Do you remember what I taught you? Al-Baqarah takes us into a room like that. An old man, his sons gathered around the bed, and one question. Today: what will you worship after me.
screen: `THE LAST CONVERSATIONS ARE SHORT.` → `AN OLD MAN, HIS SONS AROUND THE BED.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The old man is Ya'qub, the grandson of Ibrahim, the man also called Israel. The verse before tells us Ibrahim had given his sons a charge, and Ya'qub did the same: God has chosen the religion for you, so don't die except in submission to Him. Then verse one hundred thirty-three asks the listener directly: were you there when death came to Ya'qub? And it lets us in. He says to his sons, in Pickthall's words: “What will ye worship after me?” Not what will you do with the flocks. Not who gets what. The one thing he wants to know before he goes. And they answer with a chain of names: we will worship your God, the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we submit. Notice one name in that chain. Isma'il isn't Ya'qub's father; he's his uncle, the brother of his father Ishaq. The commentators point out that Arabic, like many languages, can count an uncle among the fathers. The sons name both branches of the family in one breath, as one line of faith. In Islamic tradition, this kind of deathbed charge has a name: wasiyyah, a counsel, a will. Muslims are encouraged to write a will for their property, and many also leave words for their families about prayer, kindness, and keeping ties. Ya'qub's wasiyyah is a single question. He doesn't tell his sons what to keep. He asks them, and lets them say it in their own voices. What will you keep after me?
screen: `WERE YOU THERE WHEN DEATH CAME?` · `WHAT WILL YE WORSHIP AFTER ME?` · `A CHAIN OF NAMES, BOTH BRANCHES` · `WASIYYAH: THE LAST COUNSEL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone what you hope they keep. Sit with it first. Who will carry something of you after you: a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend? What one thing do you hope they keep? Not a possession. A habit, a way of treating people, a word, a faith. Find it, and put it into one plain sentence in your head. Then decide when you'll say it to them. The bell holds the time.
What will you worship after me. Ya'qub's last question to his sons, and their answer: your God, the God of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, one God. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT WILL YOU WORSHIP AFTER ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what will you keep after me. Today, say your one sentence to the person you thought of, or write it down for them. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: A middle people
346.hook: We made you a community of the middle way (2:143)
346.howItsDone: Muslim scholars often cite 2:143 and the hadith of the three men in Bukhari when teaching moderation in worship: steady, sustainable practice rather than extremes of devotion or neglect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what will you worship after me, and your line, what will you keep after me. Did you say your sentence to someone? Today, a word about a whole community. Day three hundred forty-six.

Al-Baqarah has two hundred eighty-six verses. Divide by two, and you land on verse one hundred forty-three. Many readers have noticed that this verse, sitting in the middle of the longest surah, is the verse about being in the middle. Whether that's design or coincidence, the Qur'an doesn't say, and scholars don't build anything on it. But it makes the verse easy to find, and it fits what the verse says. Today: wasat.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED EIGHTY-SIX, DIVIDED BY TWO.` → `VERSE ONE HUNDRED FORTY-THREE.` → `THE MIDDLE VERSE, ABOUT THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Last year you met this verse as part of the story of the qiblah turning toward Mecca. This year, look at one word. In Pickthall's words: “Thus We have appointed you a middle nation.” The Arabic is ummatan wasatan, a community that is wasat. Wasat means the middle, the center. But in Arabic the middle is also the best part: the middle of the valley, where the water runs, the middle of the family, the most honored. A hadith in Bukhari explains the word in this very verse with one other: 'adl, just, balanced. And the verse gives a reason. A middle people, so that you may be witnesses over humanity, and the messenger a witness over you. A witness has to stand where both sides can be seen. You can't see the whole field from one end zone. So what does the middle look like in a life? Bukhari tells of three men who asked about the Prophet's worship and found it less than they expected. One said: I'll pray all night, every night. Another: I'll fast every day. A third: I'll never marry. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to them and said, in effect: I'm the most mindful of God among you, and I fast and I eat, I pray and I sleep, and I marry. Whoever turns from my way is not of me. The middle isn't lukewarm. It isn't half-hearted. It's the balance that lets someone keep going for a lifetime, and see both sides clearly enough to be a fair witness. The middle way.
screen: `UMMATAN WASATAN: A MIDDLE NATION` · `THE MIDDLE IS THE BEST PART` · `A WITNESS STANDS WHERE BOTH SIDES SHOW` · `I FAST AND I EAT, I PRAY AND I SLEEP`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: avoid an extreme today. Sit, and look for the place in your life where you've drifted to one end. Working through every evening. Scrolling past midnight. Promising yourself you'll never eat sugar again. Or the reverse: doing nothing at all for something you care about. Picture the middle of it. Not zero, not everything. The amount you could keep doing for a year. Rest there for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Wasat. The middle: in Arabic, also the best and the most just. Al-Baqarah calls the Muslim community a middle nation, so it can be a fair witness. Today's word.
Your line: the middle way. Today, when you catch yourself at one extreme, take one step back toward the middle. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: Remember Me
347.hook: remember Me, I will remember you, be grateful and don't deny (2:152)
347.howItsDone: Muslims practice dhikr, repeating short phrases such as subhan Allah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar after prayer and through the day, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wasat, a middle people, and your line: the middle way. Where did you step back from an extreme? Today, a verse just a few lines after the middle, that begins with the word therefore. Day three hundred forty-seven.

Some promises take a long time to arrive. A grandmother saves for a grandchild's education, and the grandchild graduates twenty years after she's gone. A seed is planted by someone who never sits in the tree's shade. Three days ago, Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed for a messenger who would come long after them. Today al-Baqarah reaches back to that prayer, says it's been answered, and asks for one thing in return. Today: remember Me.
screen: `A PROMISE THAT TAKES A LONG TIME.` → `THE PRAYER AT THE FOUNDATIONS.` → `ANSWERED, AND ONE THING ASKED.`

segments.voice: Put two verses side by side. Verse one hundred twenty-nine, Ibrahim's prayer: send them a messenger from among them, who will recite Your verses, teach the book and wisdom, and purify them. Now verse one hundred fifty-one, God speaking to the first Muslims: We have sent among you a messenger from among you, who recites Our verses to you, purifies you, and teaches you the book and wisdom. The same four things. The prayer, and its answer, twenty-two verses apart. Commentators have noticed one change: in the answer, purifying comes before teaching. Then the very next verse. In Pickthall's words: “Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.” Therefore. Because the prayer was answered. Because the gift arrived. Al-Baqarah doesn't ask for payment. It asks for remembrance, and then for gratitude: give thanks to Me, and don't deny Me. Remembrance and gratitude, side by side, as if they were the same act seen from two angles. And it's a two-way promise. You remember; you are remembered. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari adds one detail: whoever remembers God in a gathering, God remembers them in a better gathering. Think of it: your name mentioned, kindly, in a place you can't see. Last year you learned dhikr, the practice of remembering. Today, look at where the Qur'an puts it: right after a gift that took centuries to arrive. Remembering is how you receive something that big. You were remembered first, by a prayer said over stones long ago. You remember back, and are remembered back.
screen: `THE PRAYER (2:129), THE ANSWER (2:151)` · `THEREFORE REMEMBER ME` · `REMEMBRANCE AND GRATITUDE, SIDE BY SIDE` · `REMEMBERED FIRST, REMEMBERED BACK`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a minute of dhikr. Sit comfortably. If you pray, choose one short phrase you know: subhan Allah, alhamdulillah, or Allahu akbar. Say it softly, slowly, with the breath, counting on your fingers if you like. If you don't pray, choose one person who remembered you once, when you needed it, and let their name come back to you with each breath. Either way, let the remembering be unhurried. The bell holds the time.
Remember Me. Al-Baqarah's request, right after the answer to Ibrahim's prayer: remember Me, I will remember you; be grateful, and don't deny. Today's word.
Your line: remembered back. Today, remember someone kindly in a place they can't see: mention them well to someone else. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: To Him we return
348.hook: those who, struck by loss, say we belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156)
348.carry: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
348.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or any misfortune, and many add the supplication taught in Sahih Muslim asking God for reward in the loss and something better in its place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: remember Me, and your line, remembered back. Did you mention someone kindly where they couldn't hear? Today the surah keeps reading, and the next thing it promises is a test. Day three hundred forty-eight.

A phone buzzes in a family group chat: someone's uncle has died. Within minutes the replies stack up, and if the family is Muslim, many of them are the same short Arabic line, sometimes typed out in full, sometimes just the letters. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. People who know almost no Arabic know this line. It's said at funerals, on hearing bad news, even when a phone screen cracks. It comes from al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six. Today: to Him we return.
screen: `A MESSAGE IN THE FAMILY CHAT.` → `THE SAME SHORT LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `AL-BAQARAH, VERSE 156.`

segments.voice: Read the line where it sits. Just after remember Me comes a warning, not a comfort. God says, in the next verses, that He will surely test people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and harvests. And then: give good news to the patient. Who are they? Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” Two halves. We belong to God: whatever was lost was never fully ours, and neither are we. And to Him we return: the loss isn't the end of the road. And the next verse says on such people are blessings from their Lord, and mercy, and they are the rightly guided. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows what this did in one life. Umm Salamah heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by a loss and says these words, adding, O God, reward me in my loss and give me something better in its place, will be given something better. Then her husband, Abu Salamah, died. She said the words, and she wondered: who could be better than Abu Salamah, the first family to emigrate? She said them anyway. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. She told the story for the rest of her life. Notice the line is spoken in the plural. We belong. We return. Even the one grieving alone says it as part of a we. That's why it travels through the family chat so fast.
screen: `FIRST, A PROMISED TEST` · `WE BELONG TO GOD; WE RETURN TO HIM` · `UMM SALAMAH SAID IT ANYWAY` · `SPOKEN IN THE PLURAL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it when you hear of any loss. Sit, and bring to mind one loss, recent or old, large or small. Let yourself feel it for a moment, without pushing it away. Then, if you're Muslim or wish to, say the line slowly: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. If you don't, you can hold its two halves in English: this was never fully mine; this isn't the end of the road. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
To Him we return. The words of the patient in al-Baqarah, said at every loss: we belong to God, and to Him we are returning. Today's word.
Your line: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Today, when you hear of any loss, yours or someone else's, let the line come to you. Day three hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 348 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO THINK.`

349.title: Signs for those who think
349.hook: ships on the sea, rain, winds, clouds between sky and earth (2:164)
349.howItsDone: Muslims call both the verses of the Qur'an and the features of the natural world ayat, signs, and many teachers encourage reflection, tafakkur, on rain, sky and creatures as a form of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: to Him we return, and your line, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Did the words come to you at any loss? Today al-Baqarah lifts its eyes from loss to the sky. Day three hundred forty-nine.

A cargo ship, longer than three football fields, slides into a harbor carrying the bananas you'll buy next week. Over it, a weather front rolls in from the sea: a gray wall of cloud, millions of tons of water hanging in the air, held up by nothing you can see. Then the wind turns, and the rain falls on the hills behind the town, and in a week the hills are green. You've seen all of this a thousand times. Al-Baqarah asks you to look again. Today: signs for those who think.
screen: `A CARGO SHIP SLIDES INTO HARBOR.` → `WATER HANGING IN THE AIR.` → `LOOK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred sixty-four is a list. Count with me. The creation of the heavens and the earth. The alternation of night and day. Ships that run on the sea with what benefits people. The water God sends down from the sky, bringing the earth to life after it was dead. Every kind of creature scattered across it. The turning of the winds. And the clouds, held in service between the sky and the earth. Seven things. And then the verse ends: in these are signs for people who use their reason. Two words carry the whole verse. The first is ayat, signs. It's the same word Muslims use for the verses of the Qur'an. A line of the book is an ayah, and so is a cloud. The book and the world are both read. The second word is ya'qilun, those who reason, who think. It comes from 'aql, the mind, and the classical dictionaries connect that root to 'iqal, the cord used to tie a camel so it doesn't wander off. To reason, in that picture, is to hold a thought still long enough to follow it. This verse is one of many in the Qur'an that end with a call like this: for those who think, who reflect, who understand. Faith, here, isn't asked to look away from the world. It's asked to look harder at it. Muslim scholars through the centuries, astronomers, physicians, mathematicians, often pointed to verses like this as a reason to study. Nobody has to stop at the ship or the cloud. Signs for those who think.
screen: `SEVEN THINGS, COUNTED` · `AYAH: A VERSE, AND A CLOUD` · `'AQL: TO HOLD A THOUGHT STILL` · `LOOK HARDER AT THE WORLD`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the clouds for a minute. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Find a cloud and stay with it. Watch its edge change. Notice which way it's moving, and how fast. If there are no clouds, watch whatever moves: a tree in the wind, light on a wall. Don't name it or explain it. Just look, the way you'd read a line slowly. The bell holds the time.
Signs for those who think. Al-Baqarah's list of seven: sky and earth, night and day, ships, rain, creatures, winds and clouds. Each one an ayah, a sign, like a verse. Today's word.
screen: `SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO THINK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: signs for those who think. Today, stop once for something ordinary, rain, a ship, a bird, and look at it for ten seconds longer than usual. Day three hundred forty-nine.

the cord that keeps a camel still

options: read them as signs, and think.
fork.reveal: read them: in these are signs for people who use their reason. the world is read like the book.

original.note: Arabic: a sign; also a verse of the Qur'an. plural: ayat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty verse about nature.
what it means: a list of seven signs, read the way you read a verse, by people who think.
what a scholar hears: ayah names both verse and natural sign, and ya'qilun comes from 'aql, which the lexicons link to 'iqal, the camel's hobble.

350.title: Not east or west
350.hook: righteousness is not turning your face east or west, but belief, giving, keeping promises, patience (2:177)
350.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 2:177 as a summary of faith in practice: belief together with charity, prayer, zakat, keeping promises and patience; the same word, birr, names kindness to parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: signs for those who think. What ordinary thing did you look at a little longer? Today, the end of a week, and a verse that looks at people the way yesterday's looked at clouds. Day three hundred fifty.

A few pages back, al-Baqarah told of the qiblah turning: the direction of prayer moved from Jerusalem to Mecca, and some people argued about it loudly. Which way is right? Which way is holy? Who was wrong all those years? Arguments about direction are easy to have, because they never ask anything of the person arguing. The debate could have gone on forever. Then, about thirty verses later, the surah steps over the whole argument with one sentence. Today: birr.
screen: `THE QIBLAH TURNED.` → `WHICH WAY IS RIGHT?` → `ONE SENTENCE STEPS OVER IT.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred seventy-seven, in Pickthall's words: “It is not righteousness that ye turn your faces to the East and the West.” The word is birr: righteousness, goodness, devotion. It's the same word Muslims use for kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn. Then the verse says what birr is, and it's a long, concrete list. Belief: in God, the Last Day, the angels, the book, the prophets. Giving wealth, though you love it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and to free those in bondage. Establishing the prayer and paying the zakat. Keeping your promises when you make them. And patience in poverty, in sickness, and in the moment of danger. Commentators read one phrase two ways. Giving wealth 'ala hubbihi can mean despite loving it, or out of love for God. Both are true of real giving. Notice the verse doesn't say direction doesn't matter. Muslims still face the Kaaba five times a day. It says that facing the right way isn't, by itself, goodness. Goodness is belief that shows up as giving, praying, keeping your word, and holding steady when things go wrong. Look back at the week. Builders who prayed for people not yet born. A father asking what his sons would keep. A middle people. Remembrance, loss, the clouds. Each day was a piece of this one list. Righteousness is what you do.
screen: `NOT EAST, NOT WEST` · `BIRR: GOODNESS, DEVOTION` · `BELIEF, GIVING, PROMISES, PATIENCE` · `THE WEEK, IN ONE LIST`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one promise today. Sit, and think back over the last week. What did you say you'd do? Call back, send the file, fix the shelf, visit, pay someone back. Find one you haven't kept yet. Picture yourself keeping it, today, in the plainest way. Then let the breath settle, and hold the decision quietly, like something already done. The bell holds the time.
Birr. Righteousness, goodness, devotion. Al-Baqarah says it's not facing east or west, but belief, giving, prayer, keeping promises, and patience. Today's word.
Your line: righteousness is what you do. Today, keep the promise you found, before the day ends, even if it is small and nobody but you remembers it. Day three hundred fifty.
